introduction: Part XVIII (Articles 352-360) of the Constitution deals with Emergency Provisions. These enable the Central government to effectively handle any abnormal situation. Additionally, Part XIX contains miscellaneous articles protecting top officials, and Part XX deals with constitutional amendments.

core_concepts.title: National Emergency (Article 352)
core_concepts.description: The President can declare a National Emergency if the security of India or a part of it is threatened by war, external aggression, or 'armed rebellion'.

core_concepts.title: President's Rule (Article 356)
core_concepts.description: Also known as State Emergency or Constitutional Emergency. It is imposed if a state government cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution.

core_concepts.title: Financial Emergency (Article 360)
core_concepts.description: The President can proclaim a Financial Emergency if he is satisfied that the financial stability or credit of India is threatened. It has NEVER been imposed in India.

core_concepts.title: Amendment of the Constitution (Article 368)
core_concepts.description: Found in Part XX, this article grants the Parliament the power to amend the Constitution and lays down the procedure for doing so.

important_entities.name: Weimar Constitution of Germany
important_entities.significance: The feature of suspending Fundamental Rights during an Emergency was borrowed from the Weimar Constitution of Germany.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Exams frequently ask how many times Financial Emergency has been declared in India. The answer is always Zero (0).

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: There is a gap of exactly 4 articles between the three types of emergencies: National (352), State (356), and Financial (360).

exam_strategy_tips: Memorize the exact phrasing of the three emergencies. Direct matching questions based on 352, 356, and 360 are incredibly common.
Remember that only the President of India has the authority to proclaim any of the three emergencies.
